date: c. 1789-1806 (letters undated in the released transcriptions)
title: James Wilkinson ('Agent 13') ↔ Spanish governors of Louisiana: cipher letters in two dictionary-and-table codes, most pages unread
correspondents: James Wilkinson → Spanish governors of Louisiana / agents of the Spanish Crown (Miró, Carondelet, Gayoso; not itemised in the source), and replies
language: English (some French words in the plaintext)
shelfmark: Library of Congress, Manuscript Division, reproductions of the Archivo General de Indias, Papeles procedentes de Cuba, legajo 2374 (LoC page numbers 1524-1652, 2874-3072; 'File 1', 'File A', 'File B'); originals AGI Cuba leg. 2374
folio_note: Per the Chu/Valenti/Knight project inventory (github c2huc2hu/wilkinson data.txt): about 73 pp of ciphertext without decipherment and 28 pp with interlinear decipherment. Two systems: the '1078' code (table of ~1,240 numbered words with caret, plus page.row dictionary references with one or two bars for the column; dictionary ~780 pp x 2 cols x 29 rows) and a different '1096' system. Unsolved pages: LoC 1524, 1576-1583, 1598-1600, 1630-1631, 1642-1643, 2874, 2888-2890, 2895-2898, 2907-2909, 2930, 2943-2946, 2951-2953, 2962-2965, 2972, 3044-3047; decipherments for 1614-1624 and 1635-1637 exist (LoC 2975-2989, 3014-3018) but the project did not have the scans.
status: Partly read. Chu, Valenti and Knight (EMNLP Findings 2020, arXiv 2010.04746) recovered 75.1% of cipher-word tokens on a held-out 500-token excerpt (LoC 3044-3045) by a known-plaintext wordbank from the deciphered pages plus a neural LM; the dictionary itself was never identified and the 1096 system was not attacked. Not in the repo (known.py: no hits for 2374, Papeles de Cuba, Wilkinson cipher). Not on DECODE as far as checked.
why: Wilkinson's paid espionage for Spain while commanding the US Army is a major early-republic affair; the unread letters would document what he sold and when, including the Burr period.
score_note: Scored from the Chu/Valenti/Knight 2020 paper and their released transcriptions during the Oct 2026 Library of Congress sweep (research/us_loc/); LoC scans not viewed (not online at loc.gov as far as found)
verify: Get the LoC reproductions of AGI Cuba leg. 2374 (or AGI originals via PARES, Papeles de Cuba 2374); identify the dictionary (c. 1790s English dictionary of ~780 pp, 2 cols, 29 rows: candidates Entick's New Spelling Dictionary editions, Johnson abridgements); bank the 27 deciphered-but-unbanked pages; attack the 1096 system from the 1614-1624/2975-2989 pair.
prior_art: partly read: Chu, Valenti & Knight 2020, 75.1% tokens on one excerpt; dictionary unidentified (checked 28 Oct 2026: arXiv paper, GitHub repo, web search; no later full reading found)

title: Theodore Roosevelt → John Hay, coded telegram (no decoding noted)
shelfmark: Library of Congress, Manuscript Division, Theodore Roosevelt Papers (TR Center image LC reel 413, frame 0026)
folio_note: 1 typed page; Theodore Roosevelt Center record o266250 describes it only as 'Coded message'
status: TR Center catalogue gives no plaintext and no decoding; probably the State Department or a commercial telegraphic code of 1903, so a codebook should read it. Hay's received copy (Hay Papers, LoC/Brown) may carry the decode. Not in the repo (known.py). TR Center image server refused a scripted download (S3 AccessDenied), not viewed.
why: Presidential coded traffic to the Secretary of State in May 1903 (Panama treaty / Alaska boundary period); short, low weight.

title: Alexander Graham Bell → Mabel Hubbard Bell, 'Unicode' code telegram quoted in a letter, left for her to decipher
correspondents: Alexander Graham Bell → Mabel Hubbard Bell
shelfmark: Library of Congress, Manuscript Division, Alexander Graham Bell Family Papers, magbell.04100117
folio_note: Five code words plus a name: 'Roboro, Diallage, Siquando, Adalligo, Promulgo Bert.' signed 'Signinas' (By the People transcription); the letter says he sent 'the following unicode message which you may have some fun in deciphering'
status: Commercial phrase code ('The Unicode Universal Telegraphic Phrase Book', 1886 onward); no decoding in the transcription. Not in the repo. A family telegram, trivial once the codebook edition is found.
why: Small private use of a commercial code by Bell; mainly a quick, checkable code-book exercise.
score_note: Scored from the LoC transcription during the Oct 2026 Library of Congress sweep (research/us_loc/); image not viewed
verify: Look the five words up in The Unicode (1889 or 1898 ed., archive.org); confirm spellings on the image.
